lessons.title: Communicable diseases
lessons.summary: Meet the four types of pathogen and the diseases they cause, then see how the body keeps them out, how white blood cells fight back, and how vaccines and drugs help.
objectives: I can describe how bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists cause disease and how they spread.
I can describe named diseases including measles, HIV, salmonella, gonorrhoea, malaria and rose black spot.
I can explain how the body's non-specific defences and white blood cells protect against pathogens.
I can explain how vaccination gives immunity and how antibiotics and painkillers differ.
I can describe how new drugs are discovered and tested.

activities.title: Pathogens and how they spread
activities.content:
## What is a pathogen?

A **pathogen** is a microorganism that causes an infectious (communicable) disease. Pathogens can infect plants as well as animals. There are four types:

| Type | How it causes harm | Example diseases |
|---|---|---|
| **Bacteria** | Reproduce rapidly inside the body and release **toxins** (poisons) that damage tissues | Salmonella, gonorrhoea |
| **Viruses** | Enter cells and reproduce inside them, then burst the cells open, causing damage | Measles, HIV, tobacco mosaic virus |
| **Fungi** | Grow on or in tissues, sometimes producing spores | Rose black spot |
| **Protists** | Single-celled organisms, often with a complex life cycle involving a carrier | Malaria |

Viruses are much smaller than bacteria and cannot reproduce on their own.

## How pathogens spread

- **Through the air:** droplets from coughs and sneezes (measles).
- **In water:** drinking contaminated water (cholera).
- **Direct contact:** touching infected people, animals or surfaces; sexual contact (gonorrhoea, HIV).
- **In food:** eating contaminated food (salmonella).
- **Vectors:** animals such as mosquitoes carry the pathogen from one host to another (malaria).

Spread can be reduced by good hygiene (hand washing), clean water supplies, isolating infected people, destroying vectors and vaccination.

activities.title: Worked example: the named diseases
activities.content:
**You need to know these six diseases in detail.**

| Disease | Pathogen | Spread by | Symptoms | Prevention or treatment |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Measles** | Virus | Droplets from sneezes and coughs | Fever, red skin rash; can be fatal | Vaccination of young children |
| **HIV** | Virus | Sexual contact, sharing needles | Flu-like illness at first; later attacks immune cells, leading to **AIDS** | Antiretroviral drugs slow it down; condoms, no needle sharing |
| **Salmonella** | Bacterium | Food contaminated with the bacteria or their toxins | Fever, stomach cramps, vomiting, diarrhoea | Poultry in the UK is vaccinated; cook food thoroughly |
| **Gonorrhoea** | Bacterium | Sexual contact | Thick yellow-green discharge, pain when urinating | Antibiotics (though resistant strains exist); condoms |
| **Malaria** | Protist | Mosquito **vector** | Recurrent fevers; can be fatal | Mosquito nets, insect repellent, draining stagnant water, drugs |
| **Rose black spot** | Fungus | Spores carried by wind or water splash | Purple-black spots on leaves; leaves turn yellow and drop; less photosynthesis | Fungicides; removing and destroying infected leaves |

**Exam tip:** if asked "why does HIV eventually lead to death", explain that it attacks white blood cells, so the immune system cannot fight other infections or cancers.

question.text: Match each disease to the type of pathogen that causes it.
question.hint: Only one of these is spread by a mosquito, and only one is a plant disease.
question.explanation: Measles is viral, gonorrhoea is bacterial, malaria is caused by a protist, and rose black spot is a fungal disease.

question.text: How do viruses damage the body?
question.hint: Viruses cannot reproduce on their own.
question.explanation: Viruses reproduce inside cells and burst them open, damaging tissues. Toxin production is how bacteria cause harm.

options.text: They reproduce inside cells, causing the cells to burst
They release toxins into the blood
They grow spores on the surface of the skin
They feed on red blood cells

activities.title: Keeping pathogens out
activities.content:
## Non-specific defences

The body's first line of defence works against all pathogens in the same way, which is why it is called **non-specific**.

| Defence | How it works |
|---|---|
| **Skin** | A tough physical barrier. Sebum (an oily substance) has antimicrobial properties. Scabs seal cuts quickly. |
| **Nose** | Hairs and sticky mucus trap particles and pathogens breathed in. |
| **Trachea and bronchi** | Lined with mucus that traps pathogens, and tiny hairs called **cilia** that waft the mucus up to the throat to be swallowed. |
| **Stomach** | Hydrochloric acid kills most pathogens swallowed in food, drink or mucus. |

## The immune system

If a pathogen gets past these barriers, **white blood cells** attack it. They work in three ways:

1. **Phagocytosis**: the white blood cell surrounds and engulfs the pathogen, then digests it with enzymes.
2. **Antibodies**: proteins that lock onto **antigens** (molecules on the pathogen's surface). Each antibody is specific to one antigen. Antibodies clump pathogens together so they are easier to destroy.
3. **Antitoxins**: proteins that neutralise the toxins released by bacteria.

After an infection, some white blood cells remain as **memory cells**. If the same pathogen returns, antibodies are made much faster and in larger amounts, so the person is **immune**.

question.text: Which of the following are ways that white blood cells defend the body? Select all that apply.
question.hint: There are three main methods; two of them start with 'anti'.
question.explanation: White blood cells engulf pathogens (phagocytosis) and produce antibodies and antitoxins. Producing mucus is a job of the airways, and platelets, not white cells, form clots.

options.text: Producing antitoxins that neutralise bacterial toxins

options.feedback: Mucus is made by the lining of the airways, not by white blood cells.

activities.title: Vaccination
activities.content:
## Training the immune system in advance

A **vaccine** contains a **dead or inactivated** form of a pathogen (or just its antigens). It is usually injected. Because the pathogen cannot cause the disease, the person stays well, but their immune system still responds:

1. White blood cells detect the antigens on the vaccine.
2. They produce **antibodies** specific to those antigens.
3. **Memory cells** are made and stay in the blood.

If the real, live pathogen infects the person later, the memory cells recognise it immediately. Antibodies are produced **faster** and in **greater quantity** than at a first infection, so the pathogen is destroyed before it can cause illness.

### Herd immunity

If a large proportion of a population is vaccinated, the pathogen struggles to find unprotected hosts, so it cannot spread easily. This protects people who cannot be vaccinated, such as newborn babies or those with weak immune systems.

### Weighing it up

- **Benefits:** diseases such as smallpox have been wiped out; measles and polio are rare in countries with good vaccination programmes.
- **Drawbacks:** vaccines do not always work in every person; there can be mild side effects such as a sore arm or a slight fever; a few people may have a bad reaction.

Vaccines only protect against the specific pathogen they were made from, because antibodies are specific.

activities.title: Worked example: reading an antibody graph
activities.content:
**A graph shows antibody concentration in the blood against time. There is a small, slow rise after a vaccination on day 0, then a much larger, faster rise after exposure to the live pathogen on day 40.**

```
antibody
level   |                      /\
        |                     /  \___
        |      _              /
        |     / \____________/
        |____/
        +---------------------------- time
         0 (vaccine)      40 (pathogen)
```

**Explain the shape of the graph.**

- After vaccination, white blood cells meet the antigen for the first time. It takes days for them to make antibodies, and only a modest amount is produced. This is the **primary response**.
- Memory cells are left behind.
- When the live pathogen arrives, memory cells recognise the antigen straight away. Antibodies are produced much **sooner** and reach a much **higher** concentration. This is the **secondary response**, and it destroys the pathogen before symptoms develop.

**Exam phrasing that scores:** *"faster"* and *"more antibodies"* are both needed to compare the two responses.

question.text: Explain how a vaccine protects a person against a disease caused by a virus.
question.hint: Start with what is in the vaccine, then describe what white blood cells do, then what happens on future infection.
question.explanation: The vaccine contains a dead or inactive form of the virus. White blood cells produce antibodies against its antigens and memory cells are formed. If the live virus enters the body later, antibodies are made rapidly and in large amounts, destroying it before illness develops.

markScheme.criterion: Vaccine contains dead / inactive / weakened pathogen or its antigens
White blood cells produce antibodies (and memory cells)
On re-infection antibodies are produced faster / in greater quantity

activities.title: Antibiotics and painkillers
activities.content:
## Two very different kinds of medicine

**Antibiotics** (such as penicillin) are medicines that **kill bacteria** inside the body without harming body cells. Different antibiotics work against different bacteria, so a doctor must choose the right one. Antibiotics have greatly reduced deaths from bacterial diseases.

Antibiotics **do not work on viruses**. Viruses live and reproduce *inside* body cells, so it is very hard to make a drug that destroys the virus without also damaging the cells. This is why a doctor will not prescribe antibiotics for a cold or flu.

**Painkillers** (such as paracetamol and aspirin) and other medicines relieve **symptoms** such as pain and fever, but they **do not kill pathogens**. The immune system still has to clear the infection.

### Antibiotic resistance

When antibiotics are used, any bacteria that happen to be resistant survive and reproduce, so resistant strains such as **MRSA** become more common. To slow this down:

- do not prescribe antibiotics for non-serious or viral infections;
- always finish the full course so all bacteria are killed;
- limit antibiotic use in farming.

question.text: True or false: antibiotics are an effective treatment for measles.
question.hint: What type of pathogen causes measles?
question.explanation: False. Measles is caused by a virus, and antibiotics only kill bacteria.

activities.title: Discovering and testing new drugs
activities.content:
## Where drugs come from

Traditionally, drugs were extracted from plants and microorganisms:

- The heart drug **digitalis** comes from foxgloves.
- The painkiller **aspirin** originates from willow bark.
- **Penicillin** was discovered by Alexander Fleming from the *Penicillium* mould.

Today most new drugs are designed by chemists in the pharmaceutical industry, although the starting point may still be a chemical found in nature.

## Testing a new drug

Every new drug must be tested for **toxicity** (is it safe?), **efficacy** (does it work?) and **dose** (how much, how often?).

1. **Preclinical testing**: on cells, tissues and then live animals in the laboratory.
2. **Clinical trials, phase 1**: very low doses given to healthy volunteers to check safety.
3. **Clinical trials, later phases**: given to patients to find the optimum dose and check it works.

In a **double blind trial**, some patients receive the drug and others a **placebo** (a dummy treatment with no drug). Neither the patients nor the doctors know who has which until the trial ends. This removes bias so the drug's true effect can be judged.

Results are **peer reviewed** (checked by other scientists) before publication to prevent false claims.

question.text:
A company has developed a new drug to treat a bacterial infection.

(a) Describe the stages of testing the drug must pass before it can be prescribed to patients. (3 marks)

(b) In the final trial, half the patients received the new drug and half received a placebo. Explain what a placebo is and why it was used. (2 marks)
question.hint: For (a), go from laboratory to healthy volunteers to patients. For (b), a placebo lets scientists compare against 'no drug'.
question.explanation: (a) The drug is first tested on cells and tissues, then on live animals, to check toxicity. It is then given in low doses to healthy volunteers to check it is safe, and finally to patients to find the optimum dose and confirm it works. (b) A placebo is a dummy treatment that looks like the drug but contains no active ingredient. It is used so the effect of the drug can be compared with no treatment, removing bias and the psychological effect of expecting to get better.

markScheme.criterion: Preclinical testing on cells, tissues and/or live animals
Low doses given to healthy volunteers to check safety / toxicity
Tested on patients to find optimum dose / check efficacy
Placebo is a treatment containing no drug / dummy pill
Used for comparison / to remove bias or the placebo effect

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Pathogens**: bacteria (toxins), viruses (burst cells), fungi, protists. Spread by air, water, contact, food or vectors.
- Know the six diseases: measles (virus), HIV (virus), salmonella (bacterium), gonorrhoea (bacterium), malaria (protist, mosquito vector), rose black spot (fungus).
- **Non-specific defences**: skin, nose hairs and mucus, cilia in the airways, stomach acid.
- **White blood cells**: phagocytosis, antibodies (specific to antigens), antitoxins. Memory cells give immunity.
- **Vaccines** contain dead or inactive pathogens; on re-infection antibodies are made faster and in greater amounts.
- **Antibiotics** kill bacteria only; **painkillers** treat symptoms. Overuse causes resistance.
- New drugs are tested for toxicity, efficacy and dose: cells → animals → healthy volunteers → patients, using placebos and double blind trials.

practiceQuestions.text: Which pathogen is spread by a mosquito vector?
practiceQuestions.hint: It causes repeated fevers and is common in tropical regions.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Malaria is caused by a protist carried between people by mosquitoes.

options.feedback: Measles spreads in droplets from coughs and sneezes.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: painkillers such as paracetamol kill the pathogens that cause an infection.
practiceQuestions.hint: Do painkillers cure a cold, or just make you feel better?
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Painkillers relieve symptoms but do not kill pathogens; the immune system clears the infection.

metadata.blanksText: Bacteria damage the body by releasing ___. White blood cells make ___ that lock onto antigens on the pathogen, and ___ that neutralise poisons.

practiceQuestions.hint: The first word is a general word for poisons; the other two start with 'anti'.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Bacteria release toxins. White blood cells make antibodies (specific to antigens) and antitoxins (which neutralise toxins).

practiceQuestions.text: Match each body part to its non-specific defence.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about barrier, trapping, sweeping and killing.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Skin is a physical barrier; the nose traps particles in mucus and hairs; the trachea has cilia that waft mucus upwards; the stomach has acid that kills pathogens.

pairs.right: Physical barrier that also produces antimicrobial sebum
Cilia waft mucus up to the throat

practiceQuestions.text: Which actions help to slow the development of antibiotic-resistant bacteria? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: Resistance develops when bacteria are exposed to antibiotics but not all are killed.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Finishing the full course kills all the bacteria, and not prescribing antibiotics for viral infections reduces unnecessary exposure. Taking antibiotics for a cold is pointless (viral) and stopping early leaves survivors.

options.text: Always finish the full course of antibiotics
Do not prescribe antibiotics for viral infections
Take antibiotics whenever you have a cold
options.feedback: Colds are viral; antibiotics have no effect and increase resistance.

options.text: Stop taking antibiotics as soon as you feel better

practiceQuestions.text: Put the stages of drug testing in the correct order.
practiceQuestions.hint: Nothing is given to a human until laboratory tests are complete, and patients come after healthy people.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Cells and tissues → live animals → healthy volunteers at low dose → patients to find the optimum dose.
order: Tested on cells and tissues in the laboratory
Low doses given to healthy volunteers
Given to patients to find the optimum dose

practiceQuestions.text: Explain why it is difficult to develop drugs that kill viruses.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Viruses reproduce inside the body's own cells, so a drug that destroys the virus is likely to damage the cells as well.

markScheme.criterion: Viruses live / reproduce inside body cells
A drug that kills the virus would also damage the body's cells

practiceQuestions.text: In a double blind trial, who knows which patients are receiving the placebo?
practiceQuestions.hint: The word 'double' refers to two groups of people being kept unaware.
practiceQuestions.explanation: In a double blind trial neither the patients nor the doctors running the trial know who has the real drug until the results are analysed. This prevents bias.

options.text: Neither the patients nor the doctors
The doctors but not the patients
options.feedback: That would be a single blind trial.

options.text: The patients but not the doctors
Both the patients and the doctors

practiceQuestions.text:
Rose black spot is a fungal disease of rose plants.

(a) Describe the symptoms of rose black spot and explain how it affects the growth of the plant. (2 marks)

(b) Describe how the disease spreads and give **one** way a gardener could control it. (2 marks)
practiceQuestions.hint: Link the leaf symptoms to photosynthesis. Fungal spores travel in water and air.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) Purple or black spots develop on the leaves, which turn yellow and drop early. With fewer healthy leaves the plant photosynthesises less, so it makes less glucose and grows poorly. (b) The fungus spreads by spores carried in water splashes or wind. It can be controlled by spraying with fungicide or by removing and burning infected leaves so spores cannot spread.

markScheme.criterion: Black or purple spots on leaves, leaves turn yellow and fall off
Reduced photosynthesis so less glucose for growth
Spread by spores in water or wind
Control: fungicide, or remove and destroy infected leaves

practiceQuestions.text: Which drug was originally extracted from willow bark?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Aspirin originates from a chemical found in willow bark. Digitalis comes from foxgloves and penicillin from a mould.

options.feedback: Penicillin comes from the Penicillium mould.

practiceQuestions.text: Explain why a person who has recovered from measles does not usually catch measles again.
practiceQuestions.hint: What is left behind in the blood after an infection?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Memory cells remain in the blood after the first infection. If the measles virus enters again, the memory cells produce the specific antibodies very quickly and in large amounts, destroying the virus before symptoms appear.

markScheme.criterion: Memory cells remain after the first infection
Antibodies produced faster / in larger amounts on re-infection so pathogen is destroyed before illness
